turns.user: My engine smells like burning oil after I drive
turns.text:
I hear you—burning-oil smell is worth taking seriously. Let me narrow down what's actually going on so we can figure out the right next step.

A few quick questions to help narrow it:

When do you notice the smell? Does it come during driving, right after you park, or both? And does it smell like burnt oil specifically (acrid, smoky) or more like oil fumes (sharp, chemical)?

Also: any visible smoke from under the hood? And have you noticed any oil spots under the car when it's parked?

These details matter because burning-oil smell can point to a few different things—some are chronic leaks that aren't urgent, some are exhaust-system issues, and some are things you want a mechanic to confirm sooner. The pattern of when it happens tells us a lot.

turns.user: Mainly after long highway drives — no smoke anywhere, no leaks I can see
turns.text:
Got it — long highway drives trigger it, no visible smoke or leaks. That's a useful pattern.

A burning-oil smell after sustained highway driving without smoke or leaks usually points to one of two things: either oil is reaching hot engine surfaces (valve cover gasket seep, rocker cover leak, a small drip onto the exhaust manifold) or there's some unburned oil vapor in the combustion chamber that only shows up under sustained load. The N63 twin-turbo in your M550i can develop slow seeps from gaskets and seals over time — it's a known tendency on the engine family — and highway driving heats everything up and stresses those seals harder than city driving does. That's the most likely culprit here.

One more clarifying question to narrow further: when you smell it, is it coming from inside the cabin (you're smelling it while driving or right after you park), or is it mostly noticeable when you open the hood or walk around the car after parking? And how strong is the smell — faint and only if you're really paying attention, or pretty obvious?

turns.user: Oil level does seem to drop a bit between changes too
turns.text:
That's useful — oil consumption between services combined with the burning-oil smell points toward internal combustion, not just a surface seepage issue. Here's what's likely happening:

When oil gets into the combustion chamber (usually through worn piston rings, valve seals, or PCV system issues), it burns along with the fuel. You'll see two signs working together: the smell itself, and the level dropping faster than normal. On your M550i with the N63 twin-turbo, this is actually a known concern across that generation — the N63 has a reputation for higher oil consumption than its atmospheric predecessors, and early examples sometimes developed ring wear or seal degradation.

The burn rate you're describing — noticeable drop between services — suggests it's more than just the minor seepage that all engines have. The question now is whether it's accelerating or stable. If the drop is consistent turn-to-turn, it's chronic but manageable; if it's getting worse, that's a flag to address sooner.

Next step: A Diagnostic Scan will let a mechanic pull the engine codes and check the PCV system, fuel trim, and other combustion signals that tell us whether this is rings, seals, or a system fault. They can also log how much oil you're actually losing per mile, which gives you a real picture of urgency. Want me to set up a Diagnostic Scan?
